title: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market
author: OECD

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source describes proposed EU liability reforms responding to AI opacity, evidentiary burdens and victim compensation, but it does not assess whether human oversight provides effective control, requires independent verification or preserves expertise. It therefore informs the cluster’s liability discussion without taking a discernible position on its principal proposition.
qs: However, the opacity and complexity of AI systems can make it difficult and expensive for victims to build cases and explain in detail how harm was caused.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography entries rather than substantive OECD analysis. They identify research on AI implementation, labour-market effects, surveillance and exam performance, but do not reveal whether the OECD accepts, qualifies or rejects the cluster’s account of organisational choices, professional power and redistributed status in legal work.
qs: (2023), “The impact of AI on the workplace: Evidence from OECD case studies of AI     [20]     implementation”, OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers, No.

(2021), “Contract lawyers face a growing invasion of surveillance programs that        [58]    monitor their work”, The Washington Post,    https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2021/11/11/lawyer-facial-recognition-monitoring/    (accessed on 10 January 2022).

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The OECD accepts that task-level productivity gains do not mechanically determine aggregate employment and materially develops the proposition by identifying price pass-through, demand elasticity, displacement and reinstatement as the channels that determine labour-demand effects. It also adds a policy framework focused on diagnosing which mechanisms and worker groups are affected.
qs: Finally, the productivity effect depends on the share of the cost savings from AI that are passed along to customers in the form of lower prices and the elasticity of demand for the final product.7 To summarise, there are two key questions concerning the effect of AI on aggregate employment.

The effects that are dominating point to which groups’ employment prospects may be most harmed by AI and suggest specific points where policy makers may wish to intervene to ensure that the cost savings from AI do not result in lower demand for labour (see Section 3.3 for a discussion of policies).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The OECD accepts the cluster’s core account: AI exposure does not imply wholesale replacement, effects arise through task redesign, and value and safety depend on skills, informed human oversight, implementation and continuing evaluation. It materially extends the proposition by adding worker voice and social dialogue as mechanisms for selecting technologies, shaping implementation and defining training needs, while cautioning that current employment and productivity evidence is provisional and not readily generalisable to legal work.
qs: The measure is theoretically ambiguous with respect to whether the overlap between progress in AI and the abilities required in a job means “risk of displacement”, or if AI will be complementary.

The main findings  are:      •   Social partners can facilitate the use of AI by helping to decide which AI technologies are          adopted, facilitating their introduction, and defining training needs.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The OECD supports the cluster’s core distinction between assisted task performance and labour-market outcomes. It reports productivity gains concentrated among less-experienced workers while finding no significant employment decrease in early evidence, yet cautions that narrow applications, early adoption and future displacement risks prevent broader conclusions about careers or inequality.
qs: The researchers find that the gains in productivity mostly accrue to the least experienced  workers, suggesting that the generative AI application infers and implicitly conveys the behavioural  patterns of the most productive customer support workers to those who are least skilled or experienced.

Empirical          studies using cross-country variation in AI exposure, or studies using within-country variation by          local labour markets, do not find any statistically significant decrease in employment.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The OECD excerpts support the cluster’s caution against inferring performance gains from isolated coefficients. Because the outcome headings, units, definitions and explanatory notes are missing, the mixed AI-adoption and worker-representation coefficients cannot establish whether performance improved, which skill dimension was affected or whether any effect was causal.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The OECD strongly supports the cluster’s core proposition that workable AI governance should combine enforceable safeguards with adaptable guidance, risk differentiation and implementation capacity while avoiding unnecessary barriers to beneficial adoption. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that policy activity is not proof of effectiveness, calling for comparative assessment of what works.
qs: Additionally, since soft and hard law both have benefits and drawbacks, a well-co-ordinated combination of both may be necessary to effectively ensure that AI policies are enforceable and easy to comply with, while staying up to date with the latest developments in AI.
Finally, as countries increasingly take policy action, timely, rigorous, evidence-based, and comparative assessments will be key to determining what works, and where legal gaps remain.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The OECD supports the cluster’s core distinction between task automation or exposure and net employment outcomes. It argues that productivity, displacement, reinstatement, pricing and demand jointly determine labour demand, while urging analysis of the mechanisms and affected groups. It does not, however, provide evidence specifically on stable unemployment or reduced junior hiring.
qs: Artificial intelligence will automate certain tasks, but the net impact on employment is ambiguous  The most basic building block for understanding the impact of AI on labour demand is tasks.

Broadly, is AI increasing or decreasing labour demand in the aggregate with all channels (productivity, displacement and reinstatement) included?8 More narrowly, when tasks are automated with AI, which effect is dominant: the productivity or displacement effect?9 Although the first question is often the first order point of concern, policy makers should pay careful attention to which effect is driving the results.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The OECD supports the cluster’s cautious separation of measured task gains from broader conclusions: it reports productivity improvements, often concentrated among less-experienced workers, while warning that narrow applications may not generalise across firms. It does not directly assess durable skill formation, so its support for that part of the proposition is indirect.
qs: Emerging evidence shows that generative AI produces productivity gains and  equalises performance between workers in the same roles  Emerging research on the effect of generative AI applications in the workplace finds that they increase  productivity and often increase the performance of the least experienced or lowest skilled workers.

worker productivity is consistent with emerging studies of adoption of generative AI applications in the workplace, although these applications tend to be quite specific in scope, and it is too soon to see how they generalise to a wider set of firms (see Box 4.2).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The OECD supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI is presently changing tasks and workflows more clearly than aggregate employment, while bounded productivity gains do not establish broad automation. It also reinforces the need for human review, skills, training and organisational adaptation, though its evidence is economy-wide and offers limited direct support on legal apprenticeship, pricing or access to justice.
qs: However, according to workers’  own accounts, so far, the greatest impact of AI has been felt mostly through changes in the tasks they  perform in their current roles as well as changes in the working environment.
In all cases, it needs to be prompted correctly and its output must be reviewed.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that productivity gains vary by worker and context rather than following automatically from AI access. It reports strong gains concentrated among less-experienced customer-support workers while cautioning that these narrowly scoped findings may not generalise across firms; its survey evidence also shows perceived benefits differing by education and occupation.
qs: The researchers find that the gains in productivity mostly accrue to the least experienced  workers, suggesting that the generative AI application infers and implicitly conveys the behavioural  patterns of the most productive customer support workers to those who are least skilled or experienced.

worker productivity is consistent with emerging studies of adoption of generative AI applications in the workplace, although these applications tend to be quite specific in scope, and it is too soon to see how they generalise to a wider set of firms (see Box 4.2).

st.t: Wage adjustment: Timing matters beyond headline increases
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that purchasing-power protection depends on adjustment timing, frequency, indexation design and institutional coverage rather than nominal increases alone. It also substantiates the cluster’s cautions about implementation delays and cross-country comparability without ranking wage-setting models.
qs: Some of the differences across OECD countries in the timing, frequency, and size of the nominal increases are linked to different uprating procedures (see Table 1.2).
In other countries, the minimum wage is adjusted annually or biannually but with a slightly longer delay which may make a difference in times of high and/or rising inflation.

st.t: Wage inflation: Headline increases overstate aggregate effects
st.an: The OECD source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: its conditional simulations indicate limited aggregate wage effects from minimum-wage increases. It also supplies the cluster’s central qualifications—cross-country variation due to coverage and wage distributions, possible underestimation from stronger spillovers and indexation during high inflation, and the need to assess consumer-price pass-through separately.
qs: This exercise suggests that a minimum wage increase of 1% can be expected to have an effect on aggregate wage growth between 0.03% (in the United States, using the share of minimum wage earners of state-level minimum wages) and 0.2% (in France).

st.t: Wage resilience: Predictability competes with policy discretion
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: regular adjustment can preserve low-paid workers’ purchasing power, while indexation improves predictability but constrains policy judgement and may compress wage differentials. It also substantiates the cluster’s emphasis on timing, exceptions, incomplete coverage and measurement limits rather than universal protection.
qs: Automatic indexation, more specifically, may also increase visibility and transparency for firms, which can more easily anticipate future increases,39 as opposed to discretionary increases.

However, it also reduces the scope for governments, social            partners or commissions to exercise judgement on future increases and could lead to an            excessive compression of the wage distribution if other wages are not raised, with consequences            both for individual careers, and for the design of redistribution policies.

st.t: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation
st.an: The OECD directly supports the cluster’s contingent account: workplace outcomes vary with implementation and worker voice, while consultation is associated with better reported conditions but is not established as a causal safeguard. It also supports continuing oversight, collective bargaining and regulation to address algorithmic-management risks.
qs: For example, workers in companies that consulted workers or worker representatives are 9 percentage points more likely to say that AI had improved their health and safety, compared to workers in companies that did not consult workers or workers representatives.

Although the analysis controls for an extensive set of variables, it remains descriptive and mostly serves as a motivation to investigate further any causal relation between workers’ voice and the AI transition.

kp.k: AI exposure is not equivalent to occupational automation
kp.d: The report distinguishes overlap between AI capabilities and occupational tasks from the likelihood of automation. High-skilled, white-collar occupations are highly exposed to advances in non-routine cognitive capabilities, including legal activities, but retain skills that are bottlenecks to automation. Figure 3.4 places legal occupations among those least at risk when AI and other automation technologies are considered together. Early language-model exposure estimates broadly reproduce the high-education, high-pay exposure pattern, but had not yet been externally validated.
qs: However, progress in the capabilities of AI is not equivalent to the probability of automation.
The net effect is that high-skill occupations, although more exposed to recent progress in AI, are still some of the least at risk of automation.

Occupations in finance, medicine and legal activities which often require many years of education, and whose core functions rely on accumulated experience to reach decisions, may suddenly find themselves at risk of automation from AI.
However, these estimates are based on the early assessments of the researchers, and they have not yet been validated on external data.

kp.k: Task displacement competes with productivity and new-task creation
kp.d: The report's task-based framework treats AI's net employment impact as theoretically ambiguous. Automation displaces labour, cost savings can stimulate demand for remaining tasks or other firms' outputs, and new tasks can create jobs. These mechanisms must be distinguished from direct augmentation, where workers perform existing tasks more efficiently. Whether productivity effects outweigh displacement depends partly on price reductions and the responsiveness of product demand, rather than technical capability alone.
qs: AI can affect labour demand by automating certain tasks, complementing humans in completing existing tasks, but also creating new tasks.
The productivity effect is a product of the induced demand for tasks or jobs generated from the cost savings of automation.
Finally, the productivity effect depends on the share of the cost savings from AI that are passed along to customers in the form of lower prices and the elasticity of demand for the final product.

kp.k: Aggregate employment losses were not yet demonstrable
kp.d: The reviewed evidence largely predates the latest generative AI wave. Felten, Raj and Seamans find no employment-growth effect during 2010–16; Acemoglu et al. find no statistically significant employment effects across US industries during 2010–17 or occupations through 2018. However, their vacancy analysis finds reduced hiring for jobs without AI skills in more-exposed firms and increased AI-related vacancies. A study of sell-side equity analysts also reports displacement. The report therefore distinguishes negligible aggregate effects from potentially consequential effects within particular jobs and firms.
qs: Studies examining the effect of AI on aggregate employment have so far found little to no effect on employment.
Although employment may not (yet) have declined because of AI, firms more exposed to artificial intelligence tend to hire less in jobs not requiring AI skills.
However, the authors also find a strong effect of AI on the growth of AI-related vacancies, which can be interpreted as evidence of a strong reinstatement effect.
Yet more research is clearly needed on this issue.

kp.k: Attrition and implementation delays can conceal displacement
kp.d: Low adoption, organisational adaptation and retention of existing staff help explain small observed employment effects. A US business survey found 3.2% of firms used AI during 2016–18. OECD case studies describe firms reducing staffing gradually through retirement and voluntary departures rather than immediate layoffs. Retaining workers can also insure against AI underperformance. The productivity J-curve provides a possible explanation: complementary investment initially raises costs before effective deployment produces gains, but future effects remain uncertain.
qs: Firms may keep affected workers within the firm and allow natural attrition to decrease employment levels over time.
Retaining workers after AI adoption, and by extension their accumulated firm-specific human capital, provides insurance in the case AI applications underperform their projected benefits
Firms’ adoption of AI is just beginning, and overall penetration rates are still low.
Any negative employment effects of AI may therefore take time to materialise.

kp.k: The 27% estimate concerns broad automation risk
kp.d: The report estimates that occupations in the highest-risk group account for 27% of employment on average across the OECD countries in its sample, using 2019 employment and a 2021 expert survey on automatability. This covers AI and other automation technologies, not forecast job losses from generative AI. The underlying exercise assessed 98 skills and abilities and identified the top quartile of SOC 3-digit occupations. Construction, farming and production occupations face greater risk than many highly AI-exposed professional occupations.
qs: On average across OECD countries in the sample, the occupations at the highest risk of automation account for 27% of employment
The SOC 3-digit occupations at highest risk of automation (top quartile).
The results are based on a survey of experts who evaluated the degree of automatability for 98 skills and abilities.
The study does not only focus on AI technologies but extends to other automation technologies

kp.k: Workplace findings have important sampling and timing limitations
kp.d: The OECD commissioned surveys between mid-January and mid-February 2022 covering 5 334 workers and 2 053 firms in manufacturing and finance across Austria, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, the United Kingdom and the United States. Employers were surveyed by telephone and workers through compensated online panels. The case-study programme included Japan and involved 90 firms and 325 interviews, including limited energy and logistics cases. Findings reflect reported experiences, largely precede generative AI diffusion and cannot capture workers who left following adoption.
qs: The OECD commissioned two surveys between mid-January and mid-February 2022.
A total of 90 firms participated in the project.
Across the 90 firms, 325 interviews were held as part of the case studies: 147 in finance, 154 in manufacturing and 24 in the energy and logistics sectors.
they only capture the perceptions of workers who are employed after AI adoption.

kp.k: Generative AI improves performance in specific task studies
kp.d: Box 4.2 reports emerging evidence rather than economy-wide productivity effects. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2023) find 14% higher customer-support productivity, measured as calls resolved per hour, with gains concentrated among less-experienced workers. Noy and Zhang's writing experiment finds faster completion and improved quality, particularly for poorer initial performers; stronger writers saved time without quality improvements. Peng et al.'s coding experiment finds completion over 50% faster with Copilot, with benefits greatest for less-experienced programmers. The report cautions against assuming these specific results generalise.
qs: increases productivity by 14% defined as the number of calls resolved in an hour.
They find that the poorest performers from the first writing task saw quality improvements and completion time decrease after exposure to ChatGPT.
The study finds that programmers in the treated group completed the task over 50% faster than those in the control group, and that the benefits accrued most to the least experienced programmers.
it is too soon to see how they generalise to a wider set of firms

kp.k: Firm-level productivity evidence remains mixed
kp.d: Larger, more productive firms are more likely to adopt AI, but selection into adoption complicates causal interpretation. The report finds mostly modest or statistically insignificant productivity effects after accounting for firm characteristics. Babina et al. associate AI investment with sales, employment and market-value growth but not sales per worker or total factor productivity. Employer perceptions are more positive: 57% in finance and 63% in manufacturing report positive worker-productivity effects, versus 8% and 5% reporting negative effects.
qs: Although larger, more productive firms are more likely to adopt AI, evidence for a positive causal relationship between AI and productivity is so far tenuous.
while sales and employment increase from AI, they increase proportionally, leading to no statistically significant changes in productivity.
When asked directly, however, employers do report that AI increases productivity.

kp.k: Specialist AI wage premiums do not establish general gains
kp.d: Workers with AI skills constituted at most 0.3% of OECD employment on average in the cited research. Alekseeva et al. estimate advertised-wage premiums of 11% within firms and 5% within the same firm and job title, with the highest premiums in management occupations. Evidence for workers exposed to AI without specialist skills is inconclusive. OECD case studies report unchanged wages in 84% of cases and increases in 15%, commonly associated with greater task complexity or newly acquired skills. Around two-fifths of surveyed workers feared sectoral wage reductions over the next ten years.
qs: they find a wage premium of 11% for job postings that require AI skills within the same firm, and 5% within the same firm and job title.
The highest wage premium for AI skills is found in management occupations
Case study interviewees most often reported that the wages of workers most affected by AI technologies remained unchanged (84% of case studies).
In fewer instances, interviewees reported wage increases (15% of case studies).

kp.k: AI can enrich tasks while intensifying work
kp.d: Among AI users in the OECD surveys, 63% reported greater job enjoyment. Case studies associate this with fewer repetitive administrative tasks, broader responsibilities, more customer interaction and improved decision support. Yet 75% of surveyed AI users in finance and 77% in manufacturing reported faster work pace. Removing easy tasks can eliminate periods of respite and concentrate difficult work; one Canadian manufacturer deliberately retained easy tasks for this reason. Faster work did not necessarily imply greater stress where workers also gained control.
qs: Workers who use AI report higher enjoyment in their jobs.
One reason AI may be leading to greater enjoyment on the job is that AI is more likely to automate than create repetitive tasks.
AI applications may automate the “easy” set of a worker’s tasks leaving them with the same amount of work, but without the “break” afforded by the easy problems.
they purposefully did not automate all of the easy tasks so that workers could benefit from the mental health break

kp.k: Algorithmic management differs from working alongside AI
kp.d: The report defines algorithmic management as supporting or automating managerial decisions, monitoring and task allocation. Around 7% of surveyed manufacturing workers and 6% in finance reported being managed by AI. These respondents were generally less positive about job-quality effects than workers interacting with AI in other ways. Potential harms include pervasive monitoring, heightened performance pressure and reduced autonomy. Awareness-based survey questions may disproportionately identify fully automated management, while workers may not know that human managers receive AI recommendations.
qs: Algorithmic management consists of using AI to either support or automate management decisions
respondents who are subject to algorithmic management are less positive than respondents who interact with AI in another way
The constant and pervasive monitoring and data-driven performance evaluations made possible by AI can create a high-stress environment with negative impacts on mental health
they may not be aware that their manager is “merely” supported by AI in their decision making.

kp.k: Safety improvements can conflict with surveillance and privacy
kp.d: AI-enabled machinery can separate workers from hazardous operations, and monitoring can identify safety risks. Survey respondents generally reported improved mental health and, particularly in manufacturing, physical safety. However, systems collecting behavioural, physiological or interaction data create privacy and psychosocial risks. Among workers reporting AI-related collection of personal or work-process data, more than half expressed privacy concerns; 58% in finance and 54% in manufacturing worried that too much data was collected. The report also questions the reliability of some emotion-detection claims.
qs: AI implementation was reported as improving physical safety by improving the capabilities of dangerous machines
These monitoring systems, however, often entail extensive data collection and the accompanying risks to data protection.
58% and 54% in finance and manufacturing, respectively, said that they worry that too many of their data are being collected.
Several researchers, however, are questioning AI’s ability to accurately detect emotions and non-verbal cues across different cultures

kp.k: Inclusion depends on design, accessibility and bias controls
kp.d: The report identifies potential benefits from assistive technologies, translation and performance support for less-skilled workers, alongside risks from inadequate digital skills and uneven language coverage. Employers anticipated benefits for workers with disabilities but more harm than benefit for older and low-skilled workers. AI can improve consistency in hiring and evaluation, yet historical data and design choices can institutionalise discrimination. A reported recruitment study improved both hiring quality and inclusion when its algorithm explored under-represented candidates rather than relying exclusively on historical patterns.
qs: AI-powered assistive devices to aid workers with visual, speech or hearing impairments, or prosthetic limbs, are becoming more widespread
Bias in AI systems can emerge both at the data or input level and at the system level
a systematic use of biased AI systems carries the risk of multiplying and systematising bias
The results show that AI applications can improve productivity and inclusiveness, but only if they are thoughtfully designed.

kp.k: Legal capabilities require human review, not assumed substitution
kp.d: The report describes legal-contract drafting, law-exam performance and reported judicial use as examples of emerging language-model capabilities. Its discussion of a simulated bar-exam score around the top 10% cites OpenAI's GPT-4 Technical Report; the prediction that lawyers could lose a considerable share of work is attributed to Hirani rather than established by OECD employment data. The report emphasises false or superficial outputs, correct prompting and human review. It does not provide measured legal-sector employment losses or legal-service pricing effects.
qs: It can write legal contracts, summarise the literature and accumulated knowledge on a particular subject, write and debug computer code, translate among languages, and even do arithmetic.
including passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers (OpenAI, 2023[11]).
lawyers are another profession where AI is expected to replace a considerable share of human work (Hirani, 2023[26]).
In all cases, it needs to be prompted correctly and its output must be reviewed. Human intervention thus remains crucial.

kp.k: AI changes skills beyond specialist technical expertise
kp.d: The report distinguishes skills for developing and maintaining AI from those needed to use it. Development requires combinations of programming, statistics and data skills alongside creative problem-solving, communication and management. Users generally need basic digital skills, elementary AI knowledge, analytical judgement and interpersonal skills rather than expert coding. Some adopters reported no change in skills: 57% in finance, 48% in manufacturing and 60% of case-study firms. The report notes that early adopters may already possess necessary skills, while task reallocation can increase reliance on existing expertise.
qs: The shift in skill needs is much broader
Only in few cases does the use of AI applications require specialised AI knowledge or digital or data science skills.
AI adoption affects the order and relative importance of pre-existing tasks rather than change or add new tasks
AI adopters are a selected sample of employers that are able to implement AI precisely because their workforce possess the necessary skills.

kp.k: New roles train, explain and maintain AI systems
kp.d: The report recounts Wilson, Daugherty and Morini-Bianzino's 2017 prediction of trainers, explainers and sustainers, then connects it to emerging OECD case-study roles. These include preparing data, training models, explaining outputs to non-specialists, monitoring accuracy and detecting biases or mistakes. Such work is not uniformly technical: some training involves interpersonal understanding, and explanation requires communication. A French banking and insurance case describes staff checking continued predictive performance and identifying when models and data require modification.
qs: These new roles are already emerging in firms implementing AI.
The new job profiles are not clearly defined yet
“sustainers” will check that AI systems are working as intended, detecting biases, fakes and mistakes
They will monitor algorithms’ outcomes, and ensure they continue to work as intended over time, as the technology, data and environment change.

kp.k: Training must include managers and vulnerable workers
kp.d: Among firms reporting AI-induced skill changes, retraining or upskilling was the most common response: 64% in finance and 71% in manufacturing. Nevertheless, around 40% of surveyed employers identified insufficient skills as an adoption barrier. The report recommends AI literacy across education and lifelong learning, specialist pathways combining formal education and practical experience, and targeted support for older and low-skilled workers. Managers also need knowledge of AI limitations, organisational redesign and human oversight. Government intervention is proposed for information gaps, wider social benefits and workforce diversity, while evidence on training effectiveness remains limited.
qs: Training is the most common response to changing skills needs due to AI
Understanding what AI systems can and cannot do is key to assess where and how the innovation could be used in a company
Robust systems and mechanisms need to be developed and maintained to ensure human oversight of algorithmic decision-making and management.
There is also very little evidence on the effectiveness of policies for AI skills development.

kp.k: AI-assisted learning offers personalisation but risks skill erosion
kp.d: AI can help identify labour-market skill requirements, construct individual skill profiles, recommend career transitions and personalise training. The report gives examples from the Flemish public employment service and language-learning platforms. It also warns that training costs, digital-skill requirements, bias and data protection can restrict inclusion. Generative tools can assist teaching materials, but are not necessarily designed for learning or social interaction. The possibility that automated essay-writing weakens learners' writing and knowledge is presented as a concern, not a measured educational outcome.
qs: AI can help assess skill needs, build individuals’ skill profiles, identify appropriate training courses, find viable job transitions and select appropriate training to facilitate these transitions.
Another risk is that the use of AI-powered educational tools may modify the skills that learners acquire.
if students use it to write essays and complete exams, this may lead to a decrease in their written expression skills and knowledge.
The fixed costs related to AI adoption may exacerbate inequalities between small and large actors

kp.k: Employment law provides foundations but leaves AI uncertainties
kp.d: As of publication in 2023, the report treats discrimination, privacy, labour rights and occupational safety legislation as foundations for workplace AI governance, while noting limited case law and uncertain coverage. It discusses the Italian Deliveroo algorithm ruling as an application of existing anti-discrimination law and a New Zealand dismissal decision involving an unexplained psychometric assessment. Employment power imbalances complicate genuinely voluntary consent. The report recommends monitoring case law and adapting legislation rather than assuming either that existing laws are sufficient or that AI operates outside them.
qs: existing anti-discrimination legislation is usually not designed to be applied to AI use in the workplace, and relevant case law is still limited.
it is uncertain whether meaningful consent can be obtained in situations of power asymmetry and dependency, such as job interviews and employment relationships.

Since the algorithm information (including whether it was AI per se or a less complex algorithm) was not available to the employee, they were denied the right to “an opportunity to comment” before the decision is made
Case law applying anti-discrimination legislation to AI will need to be monitored

kp.k: Trustworthy AI requires explanation, accountability and meaningful oversight
kp.d: The report recommends combining flexible soft law with enforceable obligations addressing transparency, explainability, safety and accountability. Its discussion of the EU AI Act, Canadian AIDA and US Algorithmic Accountability Act concerns proposals at the report's 2023 date, not enacted regimes. Employment-related AI could attract risk-based requirements, human oversight and auditing. However, the legal responsibilities of humans supervising AI remained uncertain, as did adequate audit design. Liability concerns also deter adoption; the report stresses clarity across developers, suppliers and users, including cross-jurisdictional arrangements.
qs: a well-co-ordinated combination of soft law and enforceable legislation (or “hard law”) may be needed
as of yet, the terms “human in the loop” or “human on the loop” have no fixed legal meaning or effect
How algorithmic audits should be conducted to ensure they contribute to trustworthy AI is still an area of active research
A lack of clear accountability limits the potential for the diffusion of trustworthy AI in the workplace.

kp.k: Worker consultation is associated with better adoption outcomes
kp.d: OECD surveys associate consultation with more favourable reports of AI performance and working conditions. Workers in consulted firms were 9 percentage points more likely to report improved health and safety. Analysis of the 2019 ESENER-3 survey also associates worker representation with mitigation of some workplace risks, but uses broad technology proxies and cross-sectional data. The report explicitly cautions about causality, reverse causality and technological confounding. Early collective agreements address data use, algorithmic transparency, human decision-making and retraining, while limited AI expertise constrains social partners' participation.

kp.k: Policy should favour complementarity and share productivity gains
kp.d: The report rejects technological determinism and recommends skills policy, competition policy, social dialogue and review of capital-versus-labour taxation. Its argument is that tax advantages can encourage marginal labour-replacing investments with insufficient productivity benefits, while competition can transmit savings into lower prices and greater demand. Worker bargaining can distribute retained gains and support redeployment. These are policy recommendations based on the report's economic framework, not demonstrated forecasts of employment outcomes.
qs: Policy should encourage the productivity and reinstatement effects of AI keeping in mind that the various effects depend on how the technology is used.
Many economies subsidise capital through the tax code while at the same time taxing labour at much higher rates.
Competition authorities can ensure that markets are competitive and cost savings from automation translate into lower prices and higher output
Policies to empower social partners and strengthen worker bargaining power can ensure that the gains from these savings are shared with incumbent workers rather than just benefiting owners.

kp.k: AI adoption occurs amid tight markets and falling wages
kp.d: The report's broader labour-market context is distinct from its AI findings: OECD employment in May 2023 was about 3% above December 2019, and unemployment stood at 4.8%. In Q1 2023, average nominal wage growth across 34 countries was 5.6%, but the nominal-growth-minus-inflation measure averaged -3.8%, with negative differences in 30 countries. The report finds no clear price-wage spiral and argues that profits could absorb some wage recovery in several sectors and countries. It advocates regular minimum-wage adjustment, collective bargaining and targeted fiscal support; these wage developments are not attributed to AI.
qs: The average unemployment rate for the OECD stood at 4.8% in May 2023
nominal wage growth fell short of inflation by -3.8%, on average, with negative differences observed in 30 countries.
Overall, there is no indication of a price-wage spiral
In the long run, sustained real wage gains can only be ensured through sustained productivity growth.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The OECD predicts extensive task transformation across labour markets, including legal work, but distinguishes exposure to AI from automation and job loss. Its principal finding as of 2023 is that AI has changed job quality more visibly than aggregate employment.
pts.d:
This is primarily a cross-domain labour-market report. In Chapters 2–3, Stijn Broecke and Andrew Green argue that AI extends automation beyond routine work to non-routine cognitive tasks, exposing highly educated professionals, including legal professionals. Broecke's note on p. 101 attributes the expectation that AI will replace a considerable share of lawyers' work to Hirani (2023); this is a cited prediction, not an OECD estimate of legal job losses. The report describes contract writing, legal assistance, law examinations and assistance with court decisions as examples of AI capabilities or applications, without establishing equivalence to autonomous legal practice. Importantly, its separate assessment of automation across technologies places legal occupations among the least at risk of automation (Figure 3.4).

Green distinguishes displacement of existing tasks, productivity-driven demand for remaining work, and creation of new tasks and jobs. Their combined employment effect is theoretically ambiguous. The empirical synthesis finds little evidence of significant aggregate employment reductions so far, while identifying reduced hiring outside AI-specialist roles in more exposed firms and displacement evidence for equity analysts. High-skilled workers have generally experienced relative employment gains despite greater AI exposure.

In Chapter 4, Green, Angelica Salvi del Pero and Annelore Verhagen report substantial wage premiums for specialist AI skills but limited or inconclusive wage effects for the much larger population exposed to AI without specialist skills. Firm-level productivity effects are modest or inconclusive after accounting for observable differences between adopters and non-adopters. Emerging generative-AI studies, however, show productivity improvements in specific tasks, frequently benefiting less experienced or initially lower-performing workers most.

AI can remove repetitive or dangerous tasks, increase engagement and autonomy, and improve perceived health and safety. Conversely, it can leave workers with more demanding tasks, intensify work, reduce social contact, and enable intrusive monitoring. Algorithmic management can improve consistency and perceived fairness but also reduce autonomy and multiply existing biases.

Julie Lassébie's Chapter 5 predicts changing demand for both technical AI skills and complementary analytical, social, communication and management skills. AI can also assist training design, personalisation and delivery, although it may exacerbate inequalities or weaken learning if poorly used. Chapters 6–7 argue that regulation, training and social dialogue can influence whether these changes benefit workers; consultation and representation are associated with better outcomes, rather than established as their cause.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The report combines econometric studies, occupational-exposure measures, expert assessments, employer and worker surveys, qualitative case studies, experiments and legal examples. It explicitly separates measured outcomes from perceptions, capability demonstrations and theoretical predictions.
pts.d:
The OECD's core workplace evidence comprises surveys conducted in January–February 2022 of 5,334 workers and 2,053 firms in manufacturing and finance across seven countries, plus 325 interviews covering 90 firms across eight countries. The case studies primarily cover manufacturing and finance, with a limited number in energy and logistics. These supply reported experiences rather than causal estimates: 63% of AI users reported improved job enjoyment; 75% in finance and 77% in manufacturing reported a faster work pace. The editorial reports that three in five surveyed workers worried about losing their jobs to AI within ten years and two in five worried about sectoral wage reductions. These are expectations, not predicted displacement or wage-loss rates.

The employment synthesis includes Felten, Raj and Seamans on US employment growth during 2010–16; Georgieff and Hyee's cross-country analysis; Acemoglu et al.'s US industry and occupation analyses through 2017–18; and Fossen and Sorgner's individual-level analysis during 2011–18. Aggregate studies generally find no statistically significant employment decline. Acemoglu et al.'s vacancy analysis finds reduced non-AI hiring in more exposed firms alongside increased AI-related vacancies. Grennan and Michaely use equity analysts' exposure to publicly available stock data as a proxy for susceptibility to AI, finding increased exits from the profession.

Exposure estimates link progress in AI applications to O*NET occupational abilities, sometimes incorporating PIAAC task data for cross-country variation. The separate estimate that 27% of employment is in occupations at highest automation risk uses a 2021 expert assessment of 98 skills and abilities, O*NET importance weights and 2019 employment shares. It includes AI and other automation technologies and identifies the top quartile of occupational risk; it is not a forecast that 27% of jobs will disappear. The report explains that the underlying study's 28% figure reflects a different country sample.

For wages, Alekseeva et al.'s job-posting analysis reports premiums of 11% for AI skills within firms and 5% within the same firm and job title. In the OECD case studies, 84% reported unchanged wages and 15% increases. For generative-AI productivity, Box 4.2 reports Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's 2023 estimate of a 14% improvement in customer-support productivity; Noy and Zhang's writing experiment finds faster completion and quality improvements concentrated among initially weaker writers; Peng et al.'s coding experiment finds completion over 50% faster with Copilot, with larger benefits for less experienced programmers.

Legal examples rest largely on cited reporting and benchmarks. The simulated-bar-exam claim on p. 158 cites OpenAI's GPT-4 Technical Report, although the surrounding prose refers broadly to ChatGPT. The report does not provide a legal-services field experiment or measured law-firm employment effect. Chapter 7's worker-representation findings use cross-sectional ESENER-3 data and the OECD workplace surveys; the authors explicitly warn about reverse causality and proxy measurement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings are an early-adoption assessment published in 2023, mostly based on evidence preceding widespread generative AI. The OECD repeatedly qualifies their applicability to future systems, other sectors and workers displaced before surveys were conducted.
pts.d:
The main employment and wage findings concern developments before or around 2022, often using considerably earlier data. The occupational-exposure measures used in Chapter 3 reflect AI progress during 2010–15. The OECD surveys predate ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. Early 2023 generative-AI experiments and exposure estimates are treated as emerging evidence, not a settled forecast. Workers' ten-year concerns are recorded as survey expectations; the report gives no date or percentage for future legal-sector job displacement. Its explicit capability forecast that AI could complete the entire PIAAC literacy and numeracy tests by 2026 is attributed to experts and concerns test performance, not employment outcomes.

Limited observed employment effects may reflect low adoption, initially modest cost savings, implementation delays, continued experimentation and firms' preference for natural attrition over layoffs. Keeping workers can also insure firms against AI applications underperforming. The productivity J-curve is presented as a theory consistent with current evidence: complementary investments and organisational restructuring may precede later gains, without a specified timetable.

Exposure means overlap between AI capabilities and occupational tasks; it is not synonymous with automation. Employment outcomes depend on technical feasibility, relative costs, creation of new tasks, the extent to which cost savings lower prices, and demand responsiveness. Early LLM exposure estimates are not yet externally validated. Claims about improved job quality are conditional on implementation and may miss workers who left after adoption. Survey and case-study findings do not necessarily generalise beyond their sectors, and cross-sectional consultation findings do not establish causation.

For language models, Lassébie explicitly states that outputs may be superficial or false, require appropriate prompting and must be reviewed. The report does not quantify the verification burden for legal work. Regulatory descriptions are likewise historical: the EU AI Act, Canadian AIDA and various US measures are discussed as proposals in the 2023 policy landscape, potentially subject to significant changes, not as current enacted requirements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Potential effects span almost all occupations, but exposure, displacement risk and access to benefits differ markedly across roles, skills, firm sizes and worker groups. The source does not offer a segmented forecast for legal-service providers or clients.
pts.d:
Legal professionals are included among highly educated workers exposed to non-routine cognitive automation. Contract drafting and legal assistance exemplify task exposure; legal occupations nevertheless appear among those least at risk in the broader automation assessment. The report does not distinguish partners, associates, paralegals, in-house counsel, ALSPs or legal clients, nor make claims about law-firm leverage, billing models or access to justice.

Managers, business professionals, chief executives and science and engineering professionals are highly exposed to AI. Workers with specialist AI skills receive substantial wage premiums, while high-skilled workers with complementary computer skills show favourable employment associations. Managers, AI developers and maintainers, and tertiary-educated workers generally report the greatest job-quality benefits. Workers subject to algorithmic management report less favourable outcomes than other AI users, especially around work intensity, autonomy and privacy.

Lower-skilled workers remain disproportionately exposed to automation across technologies and can be harder to retrain or redeploy. Older workers may face barriers from weaker digital skills and lower training participation. At the same time, generative-AI studies suggest that less experienced or lower-performing workers can gain disproportionately in particular tasks. AI translation and assistive technologies may help non-native speakers and workers with disabilities, but uneven language coverage, digital skills and access can limit benefits. Women and ethnic minorities may be harmed by biased recruitment, performance assessment or facial-recognition systems; the report also notes that women are underrepresented in the specialist AI workforce.

Large, productive and capital-intensive firms are more likely to adopt AI, partly because they can finance complementary assets and skills. Smaller firms may face adoption, data-management and compliance constraints. Platform workers face particular risks from automated allocation, monitoring and account deactivation, compounded by weaker representation or employment protections. Public employment services may use AI to improve matching and target support, while education providers can personalise training. Workers and employers with effective consultation mechanisms may experience better transitions, but the evidence is associational.
